title: Space
hookLine: a young monk skips lunch after one sentence, and that evening learns to be like space
tomorrow: why does the image stay after you close your eyes?

lines: ADVICE THAT MAKES YOU SKIP LUNCH.
cards: Some advice lands so hard you skip lunch.

A young monk named Rahula is walking into town behind the Buddha, bowl in hand, when the Buddha turns around and tells him how to see every form, his own body included: this is not mine, this I am not. Rahula stops.
Who goes begging for food after a word like that? He turns back and sits down under a tree, alone, to meditate. That evening the Buddha gives him a list of things to be like.

teach.b: Here's how the Buddha explains them. Be like the earth: people throw clean things and dirty things on it, and the earth isn't disgusted or troubled. Water washes both.
Fire burns both. Wind blows over both. And space, he says, isn't established anywhere.
When the mind is like space, pleasant and unpleasant contacts come, and they don't take hold; there's nowhere for them to stick. Buddhaghosa turns that into a disc.

teach.h: A CIRCLE OF SPACE IN A WINDOW.
teach.b: Look through a window, a keyhole or a gap in a wall, he says, and take the space inside the edges, noting space, space. At first you see the hole and its edges. Later, only a circle of space.
So, what can you see through an empty window? Nothing, and a great deal.
A window frame holds no picture, but every picture passes through it, and nothing gets stuck. That's the image for a mind that hears a compliment or an insult and doesn't grab either one.
And look at the order of Rahula's evening: earth, water, fire, air, space. The same elements this block has been gazing at, in the Buddha's own teaching.

how: In Theravada meditation the limited-space kasina takes the space seen through a window, keyhole or gap, noted as 'space, space', as the Visuddhimagga describes; the Buddha's advice to Rahula to develop meditation like space (MN 62) is studied alongside it.

o: the dark between the stars, pictured in meditation
the open gap in a window or doorway, held as an object
an empty room kept in a temple for silent sitting

p: turned back and sat under a tree
clean or dirty, it isn't troubled
the gap inside a window's edges

s: the space disc means imagining outer space
it's the open gap inside a window, keyhole or wall, noted space, space.
the Buddha told Rahula to make his meditation like earth, water, fire, air and space
space, he said, isn't established anywhere, so nothing takes hold.
a mind like space lets go only of unpleasant things
pleasant and unpleasant contacts both pass through without sticking.

games.q: under your art post, one person leaves a mean comment and another a glowing one. what does a mind like space do?
o: lets both pass through, without getting stuck on either one.
deletes the mean one and screenshots the kind one to keep.
replies to both, back and forth, until everyone agrees.
games.why: in MN 62 the point is both: pleasant and unpleasant contacts come, and in a mind like space neither takes hold.

practice: Sit or stand facing a window or an open door. Look at the space in it, not the glass and not the view, just the open air between the edges.
When something crosses it, a bird, a car, a cloud, let it pass through the frame the way it passes through space, and come back.

wordCard.voice: Space: akasa in Pali. The open gap inside a window or a doorway, where nothing lands and nothing sticks.

orig.note: Pali: space, sky (Sanskrit akasha). The disc of open space, noted space, space.

carryVoice: For the road: open space, where things pass through all day and nothing gets stuck. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 62 (Maharahulovada Sutta: on alms round the Buddha tells Rahula to see all form as 'not mine, not I, not my self'; Rahula turns back and sits under a tree; that evening the Buddha teaches him to develop meditation like earth, water, fire, air and space, for space is not established anywhere and contacts do not take hold)

Visuddhimagga 5 (the limited-space kasina: space seen through a hole in a wall, a keyhole or a window, or a hole made in a shed or a piece of leather or mat; noted as 'space, space'; the learning sign the hole with its edges, the counterpart sign only a circle of space)
